Learning Objectives
Review how the gross anatomic and microscopic structural properties of the meniscus provide
load distribution, lubrication, and stability to the knee joint.
Describe the differences between the medial and lateral menisci and the effect of those
differences on meniscal function and pathology.
Explain the role of the patient history, physical examination with meniscus-specific tests, and
imaging studies in the diagnosis of meniscal pathology.
Describe and differentiate nonsurgical and surgical management of meniscal injuries and their
outcomes.
Review the role the meniscus plays in knee stability, the relationship between the anterior
cruciate ligament and the meniscus in knee stability, and the manner in which surgical fixation
of anterior cruciate ligament and meniscal injuries relate to one another.
Describe the indications for meniscal allograft transplantation.

Overview
The medial and lateral menisci are pivotal to knee joint function.
Their unique anatomic structure provides static and dynamic stability to the knee.
The histologic and biologic composition of the menisci allows load distribution, proprioception,
and lubrication.
Advanced imaging studies can be obtained to delineate normal and pathologic menisci.
Advances in technology, instrumentation, and technique has allowed for an increased
emphasis on meniscal repair (Resource 1).
Epidemiology
With an incidence of acute meniscal tears of 61 cases per 100,000 people per year, meniscal
injuries are among the most common injuries observed in orthopaedic practice.
They occur in isolation and in combination with other knee pathologies (acute and chronic
anterior cruciate ligament [ACL] injuries, collateral ligament injuries, dislocations, etc.)
Meniscal tears are the most common indication for knee surgery.
Clinical and radiographic healing rates of 60% to 85% have been reported after repair.
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Anatomy and Biomechanics
Meniscal Anatomy
The menisci are crescent- or C-shaped and have a triangular cross section that is wider at the
periphery and tapers down toward the center of the compartment (Figure 1).
The medial and lateral menisci have anterior and posterior root attachments to the tibia that
prevent meniscal extrusion during load bearing.
Differences in the medial and lateral menisci help them perform unique functions and are
important in management (Table 1).

O-shaped (roots closer together)

Meniscal Anatomy
The medial meniscus is C-shaped, covers approximately 50% to 60% of the tibial plateau,
and has multiple firm attachment sites that limit its mobility. These attachments include
the anterior root, the deep medial collateral ligament, the posterior root, and robust
circumferential capsular attachments. In addition, the meniscotibial or coronary
ligament attaches the posteroinferior aspect of the medial meniscus to the tibia.
Because it has a more rigid attachment, the medial meniscus is a more important
secondary stabilizer to anterior translation (the primary stabilizer being the ACL). In
particular, the posterior horn of the medial meniscus has been demonstrated to act as a
brake stop mechanism to anterior tibial translation in ACL-deficient knees.1-3
Conversely, the lateral meniscus is more circular in shape and covers approximately 70%
to 80% of the lateral tibial plateau. The lateral meniscus is attached to the tibia via
anterior and posterior roots but does not have an attachment to the lateral collateral
ligament. The posterior capsular attachments of the lateral meniscus are interrupted in
the popliteal hiatus as the popliteus tendon becomes intra-articular. The anterior and
posterior meniscofemoral ligaments (Humphrey and Wrisberg, respectively) connect the
posterior horn of the lateral meniscus and the medial femoral condyle and are named
based on their anatomic relationship to the posterior cruciate ligament.
Because of these differences in attachments, the lateral meniscus has more mobility
than the medial meniscus. Although both menisci translate considerably during flexion,
this is much more pronounced on the lateral side. For example, between 15° and 30° of
flexion, the lateral meniscus translates approximately 10 mm compared with 3.5 mm for
the medial meniscus.4 In addition, the lateral meniscus has been demonstrated to be an
important stabilizer during rotation of the knee. In ACL-deficient knees, a concomitant
lateral meniscus tear leads to an increase in pivot shift.5 This is further illustrated by the
increase in pivot shift after ACL reconstruction in patients with an unrepaired lateral
meniscus tear.6

In addition to the previously mentioned attachments, the transverse intermeniscal
ligament forms a connection between the anterior horns of the medial and lateral
menisci. A posterior and medial or lateral oblique intermeniscal ligament also may be
present.
Meniscal Histologic and Biologic Composition
The unique histologic and biologic composition of the menisci allow them to function,
including proprioceptive feedback, load distribution, joint lubrication, and joint stability.7,8
Circumferential collagen fiber bundles (Figure 2)
Allow for dissipation of hoop stress
Figure 2 Schematic drawing shows the collagen fibers of the meniscus. The superficial
collagen fibers are randomly oriented to resist sheer stress. The deeper fibers are oriented
circumferentially to dissipate loads as hoop stresses. The circumferential fibers are secured
by radially oriented tie fibers. (Reproduced from Mayer SW, Bernard JA, Rodeo SA: Meniscal
injuries, in Orthopaedic Knowledge Update: Sports Medicine, ed 5. Rosemont, IL, American
Academy of Orthopedic Surgeons, 2016, pp 251-264.)

Vascular Anatomy
The meniscal vascular supply arises from the superior medial and lateral, inferior medial and
lateral, and middle genicular arteries.
Although the percentages are controversial, 50% of the meniscus is vascularized at birth,
whereas only 10% to 25% of the meniscus is vascularized in adults.
The vascularity of the meniscus affects the ability of meniscal repairs to heal.
The vascularity has been divided into three regions or zones.
Red-red
Red-white
White-white
Increased vascular supply at anterior and posterior horns
Decreased supply at popliteal hiatus

Vascular Anatomy
The menisci receive nutrient supply via two different mechanisms: vascular supply and
diffusion from synovial fluid. The superior, middle, and inferior geniculate arteries form a
well-vascularized network of synovial and capillary vessels, which in turn supply the
menisci. However, these microvascular networks begin peripherally and do not
penetrate into the entirety of the meniscus (Figure 3). The resultant gradation in
vascular supply has given rise to a definition of three zones of vascular supply: red-red,
red-white, and white-white.

Figure 3 Cross-sectional image of the medial meniscus shows the vascular supply, which
penetrates the outer 10% to 30% of the meniscus (red-red zone). The middle one-third of
the meniscus is the transition zone between the vascular and avascular regions (red-
white zone). The inner one-third of the meniscus is avascular (white-white zone). F =
femur, PCP = perimeniscal capillary plexus, T = tibia. (Reproduced with permission from
Arnoczky SP, Warren RF: Microvasculature of the human meniscus. Am J Sports Med
1982;10[2]:90-95.)
The red-red zone, so named because it is penetrated completely by the vascular supply,
is the most peripheral zone and accounts for 10% to 30% of the meniscus. The red-white
zone is a transition between the vascularized red-red zone and the completely avascular,
central white-white zone. This white-white zone is so named because it does not receive
any blood supply but, instead, is supplied via diffusion from synovial fluid during joint
loading.
In addition to the general zones of meniscal blood supply, special attention should be
paid to two areas in which this pattern differs: the popliteal hiatus and the meniscal root
attachments. Because it lacks capsular attachments, the popliteal hiatus also lacks the
robust peripheral blood supply of other portions of the meniscal body. Conversely, the
anterior and posterior roots are highly vascularized via a vascular synovial tissue.

Understanding of the three zones and special considerations is critical to proper
treatment of patients with meniscal pathology because the vascularity of the meniscus
affects its ability to heal after injury. The more peripheral the tear, the greater the
likelihood of successful healing after repair.10
Neural Anatomy
The neural supply is primarily concentrated in the meniscal horns.
It is thought to help with proprioception.

Neural Anatomy
Within the menisci, neural elements are predominantly found in the anterior and
posterior horns. The meniscal horns play an important role in stabilizing the joint by
maintaining hoop stresses and by acting as doorstops to anterior and posterior
translation of the femur on the tibia. The increase in neural supply to the meniscal horns
compared with other parts of the menisci lends support to the idea that the menisci play
a role in proprioception.
Meniscal Biomechanics
The menisci increase load-sharing across the joint, especially in deep flexion.
Increase articular congruity
Increase contact area
Decrease contact pressure
Maintain hoop stress
Increase joint stability
Provide secondary restraint to anterior tibial translation (posterior horn of the medial
meniscus)
Provide restraint to extremes of flexion and extension
Prevent synovial impingement and aid in joint lubrication
Meniscal injury alters these properties and results in dysfunction.


Meniscal Biomechanics
The most important function of the meniscus is load-sharing across the knee joint.
Because the tibia and femur are convex in nature, the tibiofemoral articulation tends
toward point-loading and large amounts of pressure in a small surface area. In the
healthy knee, menisci function to increase the contact area between the femur and the
tibia because of their congruence with the tibia and femur. Therefore, the shape of the
meniscus allows for a decrease in point-loading and contact stress on the articular
cartilage of the femur and tibia.
The tibial attachments of the meniscal roots provide a firm anchor anteriorly and
posteriorly. This allows the meniscus to stay located between the tibia and femur during
weight bearing. This positioning maintains hoop stresses on the meniscus, further off-
loading the articular surfaces of the tibiofemoral joint.
With the knee in extension, as much as 50% of the load is absorbed by the meniscus,
with the percentage of load-sharing increasing to 90% in 90° of knee flexion. Beyond 90°
of flexion, most of the force is transmitted to the posterior horns of the menisci.
In biomechanical studies, a radial tear of the medial meniscus that extends from the
inner rim to the peripheral one-third (but preserves the peripheral one-third) has not
been found to change maximum contact pressure and contact area in the knee.
However, a radial tear involving 90% of the medial meniscus results in a posterocentral
shift in peak-pressure location.
A vertical tear of the medial meniscus causes non-substantial increases in joint contact
pressure and reductions in contact area in the medial and lateral compartments of the
knee.
If the meniscus is removed completely, the articular cartilage contact stress increases by
two to three times that experienced if the meniscus is intact. Medial meniscus root tears
result in peak articular cartilage contact pressure similar to that observed after complete
meniscectomy. Such tears have been associated with the progression of osteoarthritis.

Biomechanical studies of partial meniscectomy have demonstrated increasing contact
stresses with increasing loss of meniscal tissue. Removal of the inner one-third of the
meniscus results in a 10% reduction in contact area and a 65% increase in contact stress
on the articular cartilage.
Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
Meniscal tears are unusual in patients younger than 10 years.
Most meniscal tears in adolescents and young adults result from a twisting injury or from a
change in direction.
Middle-aged and older adults can sustain a meniscal tear from squatting or falling.
Menisci degenerate over time and can create asymptomatic tears.
Associated Injuries
Although many meniscal tears occur in isolation, meniscal injury also is common to other
injuries.
Acute ACL injury is most associated with lateral meniscus injury.
Chronic ACL injury is most associated with medial meniscus injury.
Trauma, including tibial plateau fractures, also is associated with meniscal injury.

Associated Injuries
Because meniscal injuries are commonly associated with other knee injuries, surgeons
must maintain a high index of suspicion in patients with knee pain after trauma.
The medial meniscus, with its more robust capsular attachments and less mobility, is the
most important secondary stabilizer of anterior translation of the knee. Although the
ACL is the primary stabilizer, considerable interplay occurs between these two structures
in the prevention of anterior subluxation of the tibia. Biomechanical studies have
demonstrated increased ACL strain with medial meniscus deficiency and increased
medial meniscus strain with ACL deficiency.

Discoid meniscus
Discoid meniscus is a larger-than-normal meniscus from lack of central cell apoptosis in
utero.
Discoid meniscus is rare. It more commonly affects the lateral meniscus (1.4% to 15%) than
the medial meniscus (<1%; Figure 5).


Patient History
Patients with a meniscal injury localize pain to the joint line or the posterior knee and
may describe mechanical symptoms of locking or catching.
Patients with a traumatic tear tend to report an acute onset of pain during a twisting
mechanism or deep flexion. They also may report feeling a popping sensation. One-half
to two-thirds of patients experience swelling. Although studies vary widely in reporting
mechanical symptoms, such as catching, popping, and frank locking (12% to 69% of
patients in two recent studies), these physical examination findings are important
because they suggest an unstable tear pattern.12,13
Patients with chronic meniscal injuries may have waxing and waning symptoms that
correspond with symptom intensity and/or activity level. They also may experience an
acute worsening of symptoms after a specific event.

Physical Examination
In patients with an acute meniscal tear, an effusion often develops several hours
postinjury. This differs from an ACL injury, in which swelling develops rapidly within the
first few hours. Patients with effusion often report tightness in flexion and fullness or
pain in the back of the knee.
Special attention should be paid to any mechanical block to the ROM because
longitudinal bucket-handle tears may block full extension of the knee joint. Pain with
hyperflexion or hyperextension is common with meniscal injury. Pain with squatting also
is frequently noted.
Examination of the collateral and cruciate ligaments may reveal other pathologies that
affect decision making. These examinations also may provide direct information about
meniscal pathology. Although collateral ligament injuries are unstable and painful on the
tension side (eg, an MCL injury results in medial-sided pain with valgus stress), the same
examination maneuver may correspond with pain on the compression side (eg, lateral

meniscus injury results in lateral-sided pain with valgus stress) in patients with a
meniscal injury. Positive cruciate ligament testing (Lachman, anterior drawer, posterior
drawer, pivot shift tests) should increase clinical suspicion for meniscal tears because
they often are associated with cruciate ligament injury.
Palpation of the joint line may elicit tenderness in the region of a tear. Posterior horn
tears are most prevalent; therefore, the posterior joint line is a common location of
tenderness. Joint line tenderness is the most sensitive but least specific test for meniscal
injury. Therefore, a positive test should increase clinical suspicion but may not be
considered diagnostic.
Several meniscal-specific tests should be performed with analysis of pain and
mechanical symptoms. These manipulative maneuvers may produce a palpable or
audible click with localized tenderness. Each of these functional tests is designed to trap
the pathologic meniscus under axial load and rotation, and pain and/or mechanical
symptoms should be re-created.
With the patient supine or sitting, the examiner takes the knee through an ROM with
internal and external rotation of the tibia and an applied axial load.
Specifically, the medial meniscus is tested by moving the knee from flexion to extension
while applying a varus stress and external rotation, allowing the posterior medial
meniscus to contact with the femoral condyle. Conversely, the lateral meniscus is tested
by moving from flexion to extension with a valgus stress and internal rotation of the
tibia, allowing the posterior horn of the lateral meniscus to contact the femoral condyle.
With the patient in a prone position, the examiner flexes the knee to 90° and applies an
axial load to the foot. This is then combined with internal and external rotation.
Reproduction of pain or the presence of mechanical symptoms is interpreted as a
positive test.
The patient performs a single-leg squat on the affected leg to approximately 20°. This is
then augmented with rotation of the torso during flexion and extension, creating
internal and external rotation of the tibiofemoral joint.

In a patient with an isolated meniscal tear, joint line tenderness was found to be an
accurate test in 81% to 90% of patients compared with the McMurray test and 6 the
Thessaly test, which are accurate in 57% to 77% patients and 61% to 80% of patients,

In patients with a ligamentous or chondral injury, individual tests tend to lose their
accuracy in identifying meniscal pathology.12,14 However, if joint line tenderness is
combined with a positive Thessaly or McMurray test, the sensitivity and specificity
increase to that near the values noted in patients with an isolated meniscal tear.12
Neurovascular Examination
Isolated meniscal injuries are not commonly associated with abnormal vascular examination
results.
Abnormal vascular examination results should lead to consideration of other accompanying
pathology or differential diagnoses.
Imaging Studies
Radiography
Standard knee radiographs should be obtained to aid in evaluation for bone injuries or
abnormalities.
Full-length standing alignment or mechanical axis radiographs may be considered to aid in
diagnosis of root tears.
A weight-bearing radiograph is necessary to evaluate for osteoarthritis.

Radiography
Because meniscal injuries may occur in combination with other injuries, thorough
radiographic evaluation is important. Radiographic findings may provide clues to the
status of the meniscus and the environment within the knee joint. Therefore, evaluation
should include assessment for injury patterns, such as ligamentous avulsions, patellar

9/3/26, 4:42 PM
AAOS | Meniscal Injuries
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001181
18/40

malpositioning or maltracking, joint line depression, joint subluxation, and joint space
narrowing.
Evaluation via weight-bearing radiographs is critical. This may include a weight-bearing
AP or 45° PA flexion view. A right-to-left difference of at least 2 mm represents a
considerable difference that will be verified by articular cartilage chondrosis at the time
of arthroscopy.
Magnetic Resonance Imaging
MRI remains the preferred noninvasive diagnostic imaging modality for confirming meniscal
pathology.
MRI is associated with a high negative predictive value for meniscal tears (ie, a well-obtained
MRI of a knee with no meniscal pathology rarely will demonstrate a tear.)
The sensitivity and specificity of MRI vary according to the location of the tear and the type of
MRI (1.5 Tesla versus 3 Tesla) but generally are reliable.
Special care should be taken to evaluate the meniscal roots because these tears often are
overlooked on MRI. The clinician should assess for the ghost sign and the truncation sign.

Magnetic Resonance Imaging
Meniscal tears can be evaluated well on T2- weighted and proton density MRIs. Careful
study of MRI results can be useful in preoperative planning, because it can be used to
describe the nature of a tear. Special attention should be paid to the meniscal roots; root
tears are unique entities, and MRI may be less predictive in the diagnosis of root tears.
MRI grading of meniscal injury is based on the location of increased signal intensity
within the substance of the meniscus. The criteria for MRI diagnosis of a meniscal tear
include increased signal intensity extending to the articular surface from within the
normally low-signal meniscal substance; distortion of the shape or size of the meniscus,
which indicates missing meniscal tissue; or a displaced meniscal fragment (Figure 6).

MRI shows a horizontal cleavage tear of the medial meniscus at the junction of the body

&nbps;
A comparison of 1.5 Tesla and 3.0 Tesla MRI findings of medial meniscus tears
demonstrated a sensitivity of 93% to 96% and a specificity of 88% to 90%.15 The efficacy
of MRI in the diagnosis of lateral meniscus tears demonstrated less sensitivity (77% to
82%) but higher specificity (98% to 99%). Posterior meniscal root tears were less
accurately diagnosed via MRI than medial or lateral tears, with a sensitivity of 77% and
specificity of 73%.16
In identifying meniscal tears, 1.5 Tesla MRI was slightly less sensitive and specific than
3.0 Tesla MRI; however, the difference was not statistically significant.
Root tears often are missed on MRI, even by trained musculoskeletal radiologists and
orthopaedic surgeons.16,17 T2-weighted MRI findings consistent with a root tear include
a radial tear on axial images, a vertical defect on coronal images (truncation sign), and
absence of the normal meniscus (ghost sign) on at least one sagittal image. These may or
may not be accompanied by meniscal extrusion.18

Medial root tears often are isolated in older patients and more readily identified on MRI;
however, lateral root tears may be associated with acute ACL injuries and often are
missed on MRI.
Differential Diagnosis
Several large studies have demonstrated the accuracy of the clinical diagnosis of meniscal
tears to be 70% to 75%.
The differential diagnosis for meniscal tears includes intra-articular and extra-articular
diagnoses.
Possible intra-articular diagnoses
Osteochondritis dissecans
Medial patella plica
Patellofemoral pain syndromes
Loose bodies
Pigmented villonodular synovitis
Inflammatory arthropathies
Osteonecrosis
Possible extra-articular diagnoses
Collateral ligament injury
Slipped capital femoral epiphysis
Bone or soft-tissue tumor

Management
The wide range of meniscal pathologies and meniscal injury populations has led to a
correspondingly wide range of treatment options. Careful evaluation and examination of
and discussion with each individual patient should guide treatment. Not all meniscal
tears cause symptoms, and many symptomatic tears become asymptomatic with time.
Conversely, asymptomatic meniscal injuries may become symptomatic with time.
Frank discussions with patients regarding pain, injury, and current and desired activity
levels are important in determining treatment plans. Treatment options include
nonsurgical management, partial meniscectomy, meniscal repair, and meniscal allograft
transplantation.
With increased understanding of meniscal function and consequences after
meniscectomy, more effort has been made to preserve meniscal tissue if possible and to
attempt to restore meniscal function (Resource 2).

Degenerative tears that do not cause mechanical symptoms
Degenerative tears associated with considerable osteoarthritis
Short (<3 mm in length) radial tears in the white-white zone
Stable partial tears

Techniques
Nonsurgical management may include ice, NSAIDs, compressive dressings for
symptomatic effusion and/or off-loader bracing.
Physical therapy for ROM and general strengthening of the lower extremities has been
shown to be efficacious in the management of stable tears without mechanical
symptoms.
Short-term follow-up has shown that the use of intra-articular injections of corticosteroid
and viscous supplementation help with acute pain and symptoms in patients with a
degenerative meniscus tear;19-21 however, longer follow-up demonstrates an increase in
arthritis and worsening of clinical outcomes with nonsurgical management.22 The
American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline
on the Treatment of Osteoarthritis of the Knee, 2nd edition, reports inconclusive findings
regarding corticosteroid use and intra-articular biologics for the management of
degenerative knee pain. The guideline cites strong evidence against
viscosupplementation.23 Strong interest exists in the development of biologic treatment
options for meniscal injury; however, insufficient studies have been published to
conclusively determine their efficacy.
Outcomes
Nonsurgical management is designed to improve symptoms and patient activity level and will
not result in healing of meniscal tears.
Physical therapy and nonsurgical management result in patient-reported outcomes similar to
those of partial meniscectomy.24
If tears worsen or begin to result in mechanical symptoms, transition to surgical management
may be required. The findings of a randomized controlled trial showed that 30% of patients
with a nonmechanical medial meniscus tear who were randomly assigned to physical therapy
crossed over to surgical treatment within 6 months of initiating treatment.24


Outcomes
If the meniscus is removed completely, the articular cartilage contact stress increases by
two to three times that experienced if the meniscus is intact. Biomechanical studies of
partial meniscectomy have demonstrated increasing contact stresses with increasing
loss of meniscal tissue. Removal of the inner one-third of the meniscus results in a 10%
reduction in contact area and a 65% increase in contact stress on the articular cartilage.
Long-term follow-up of patients who underwent partial meniscectomy showed increases
in osteoarthritis in 35% of patients. These patients also demonstrated increased knee
function scores but variable results with regard to pain control (56% of patient-reported
improvement).29

The goal of meniscal repair is to preserve meniscal function by providing structural support
and an environment conducive to tissue healing.

Outcomes
Knees managed via partial meniscectomy demonstrated an increase in osteoarthritis at
10-year follow-up. Specifically, 37% of patients who underwent partial meniscectomy
progressed at least one grade on the Fairbank scale compared with only 22% of patients
who underwent meniscal repair.30 Results of a subsequent study showed even more
stark progression: at 8- to 10-year follow-up, 60% of patients who underwent
meniscectomy had osteoarthritis progression compared with 19.2% of patients who
underwent meniscal repair.31
These findings also have been demonstrated for meniscal root tears. At 4-year follow-up,
patients who underwent repair of a medial meniscal root tear had less progression of
osteoarthritis and better clinical scores than patients who underwent partial medial
meniscectomy.32
Although early data on meniscal repair demonstrated high short-term (16.5% versus
1.4%) and long-term (20.7% versus 3.9%) rates of revision surgery compared with
meniscectomy,30 recent review of the national insurance database, which includes much
larger patient groups (27,580 total), demonstrated a lower rate of revision surgery after
meniscal repair compared with meniscectomy (2.1% versus 5.3%) at a mean follow-up of
45 months.22 This may be partially because of longer follow-up and improved
survivorship of meniscal repair as techniques and tools continue to advance.
At a mean follow-up of 48 months after inside-out meniscal repair with vertical mattress
suturing, MRI showed a 100% healing rate for partial tears and an 80.3% rate for full-
thickness tears.33

Rehabilitation
Varies widely in the literature according to injury pattern and surgical technique
Goals of rehabilitation are to protect the repaired meniscus to allow healing. This can be
accomplished by the following:
Bracing with gradual ROM increase
Protected– or non–weight bearing
Avoidance of forced flexion and closed chain exercises during early rehabilitation
Physical therapy
Gradual return to activity
Pearls and Pitfalls
Menisci are critical to force transmission across the knee joint.
The lateral meniscus is more mobile than the medial meniscus.
Joint line tenderness is the most sensitive physical examination finding of meniscal injury.
Root tears often are missed on MRI.
Overall, medial meniscus tears are more common than lateral meniscus tears.
Lateral meniscus tears are more common with acute ACL injury, whereas medial meniscus
tears are more common with chronic ACL injury.
Meniscal tears without mechanical symptoms often can be successfully managed
nonsurgically.
If surgical management is necessary, all efforts should be made to repair meniscal tears, if
possible.
Medial repair places the saphenous nerve at risk.
Lateral repair places the peroneal nerve and popliteal vessels at risk.
Vascular supply and biologic environment determine healing potential after meniscal repair.
In meniscal allograft transplantation, fixation with the use of a bone bridge or bone plugs is
biomechanically stronger and demonstrates less extrusion than soft-tissue fixation, but it has
not demonstrated clinical superiority.
Graft-size mismatch leads to increased failure of meniscal allograft transplantation.
